records.name: Arnis (Kali / Eskrima)
records.founded: undated origin, largely oral history; fencing practice glossed in Philippine dictionaries 1613 and 1637; Doce Pares founded 1932; national martial art by law 2009
records.tagline: Blade logic drilled with rattan — a national art by law, documented in Cebu.
records.history:
Known interchangeably as Arnis, Kali, or Eskrima, the national martial art of the Philippines is one of the very few systems that teaches the weapon before the empty hand. A beginner is handed a pair of rattan sticks in the first lesson, and the reason is that the stick itself is not the point. The angles are the point; a stick, a knife, a machete, or a rolled umbrella all travel the same lines, so one drill covers every one of them. Empty-hand technique comes last, taught as the same pattern with nothing in the hand.

Almost everything before the 1600s is oral history, and the traceable record starts in Cebu with Doce Pares in 1932, Balintawak in the 1950s under Venancio "Anciong" Bacon, and Remy Presas building Modern Arnis from 1966. A 2009 law made it the national art. Its wider fame came through Dan Inosanto, who brought the stick and blade work into Bruce Lee's Jeet Kune Do, and through Hollywood, where Kali flow drills are the reason fight choreography in films like The Bourne Ultimatum and John Wick looks the way it does.

records.name: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu
records.tagline: The ground is the great equalizer — Kodokan judo, reworked in Rio.
records.history:
Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu is built on the assumption that a fight ends up on the ground whether anyone planned it or not, and that once both people are down, size matters far less than angle. A smaller grappler on their back is not losing; the guard is a fighting position rather than a pinned one, which is the idea that separates BJJ from every other grappling art. Position comes before submission, so a practitioner passes the legs, takes side control, then the mount or the back, and only then attacks the arm or the neck.

It began as judo that travelled. Mitsuyo Maeda settled in Belém around 1914 and Carlos Gracie fell into his circle by 1917. Carlos' younger brother Hélio was too small for the standard throws, so he rebuilt the art around leverage, and the academy the two opened in Rio in 1925 is the usual start date. The Gracies were never the only line; Luiz França trained under Maeda as well and passed the art to Oswaldo Fadda, whose students later beat several Gracie fighters using the footlocks Hélio had dismissed. Royce Gracie's run at UFC 1 in 1993 took it global.

records.name: Boxing
records.founded: 1867 (Marquess of Queensberry Rules); earlier codified 1743 (Broughton's Rules); ancient roots undated
records.tagline: The codified science of the fist, gloved in Victorian England.
records.history:
Boxing is the most restricted of the major striking arts, and every fighter who has borrowed from it has borrowed because of that restriction rather than in spite of it. Two closed fists, nothing below the waist, no clinching, no kicks, no throws. With no legs to check and no arms to trap, the defence has to be carried entirely by the feet and the head, which is why boxers slip, roll, and pivot to a degree no other art demands.

The sport people watch today is English. Jack Broughton wrote the first set of rules in 1743 after an opponent died in a bout, the London Prize Ring Rules replaced them in 1838 and kept fights bare-knuckle, and in 1867 John Graham Chambers drafted the Marquess of Queensberry Rules, requiring padded gloves, three-minute rounds, and a ten-count. Everything before that is ancient and disconnected, with fist-fighting in Sumerian reliefs and an Olympic event by 688 BC. Today its hands and footwork are cross-trained by strikers who have no interest in boxing itself.

records.name: Capoeira
records.founded: 16th-19th century (colonial era); first documented 1789, exact origin unknown
records.tagline: A fight disguised as a dance, forged by the enslaved of Bahia.
records.history:
Capoeira is played rather than fought, which makes it the strangest entry on any map of martial arts. Two people enter a ring of singers and clapping hands called the roda and move to whatever tempo the berimbau sets, and the instrument alone decides whether the exchange stays conversational or turns fast enough to hurt someone. The base step, the ginga, never stops, so a capoeirista is always in transition and never planted in a stance. Kicks come out of cartwheels, handstands, and low sweeps, and attacks are evaded rather than blocked, which is why so much of the art happens upside down.

It was made by enslaved and free Africans and their descendants in colonial Brazil, and the first time the record names it, in Rio court papers from 1789, it is describing a crime. An 1890 penal code banned it outright. Mestre Bimba opened an academy in Salvador in the 1930s and built Capoeira Regional, Mestre Pastinha followed in 1941 keeping the older Angola style intact, and UNESCO listed the art in 2014.

records.name: Chinese Martial Arts (Kung Fu / Wushu)
records.founded: no single founding; earliest references 5th century BC; oldest documented Shaolin fighting a 728 AD stele; surveyed nationally from 1928, state-reorganized from 1958
records.tagline: Not one art but hundreds — renamed guoshu in 1928, wushu in the 1950s.
records.history:
Chinese martial arts is a heading rather than an art. Hundreds of family styles sit under it with little in common beyond the country, and the oldest way of sorting them is geographic, with northern systems favouring long kicks, jumps, and wide stances while southern ones work short hand strikes from a low rooted base. What almost all of them share is the form. Taolu are long fixed sequences performed alone, and they carry a style's entire syllabus the way a written record would, though whether a form is a fighting method or a filing system is an argument as old as the styles themselves.

Both English names are loanwords: kung fu is Cantonese for any skill earned through practice, and wushu is Mandarin for martial art. The documented record is thin, with a 728 AD stele as the oldest evidence of Shaolin fighting and most named styles, tai chi among them, dating to the Qing or later. The Kuomintang surveyed the schools as guoshu from 1928, and the People's Republic reverted to wushu and standardized the forms from 1958. Competition wushu is now judged on difficulty and presentation rather than fighting, and practitioners still disagree over whether that preserved the arts or hollowed them out.

media.title: Once Upon a Time in China (1991)

records.name: Jeet Kune Do
records.tagline: Absorb what is useful. Discard the rest.
records.history: Founded by the legend Bruce Lee himself, Jeet Kune Do originated in Los Angeles, California during his stay in Chinatown in the mid-1960s. Authored as more of a philosophy rather than a fighting system, Lee began the "way of the intercepting fist" after a match against fellow martial artist Wong Jack Man. Even though Lee won, he felt critical of his performance due to his noticeable physical fatigue, stating that his studied classical Wing Chun taught under Grandmaster Ip Man was too rigid in stance and fighting range compared to a more modern and mobile fighter, thus prompting him to begin expanding his knowledge beyond traditional Chinese martial arts. He began to combine techniques from both his foundation of Wing Chun, western fencing (with his iconic bladed footwork and stance), as well as the biomechanics and rotational power of modern-day boxing. His philosophy was engraved in the signature motto of Jeet Kune Do, "using no way as a way, having no limitation as limitation". To learn techniques from martial arts around the world and combine them into one fluid style is hence why it is considered a philosophy rather than a martial art itself, one that is akin to modern day MMA.

records.name: Judo
records.tagline: Maximum efficiency, minimum effort.
records.history:
Judo is the art of fighting with gravity instead of against it, and unlike almost every other art on this map, nothing in it is struck. The work is to break the opponent's balance first, kuzushi, so that their weight is already falling before the throw starts, and then to steer that fall rather than lift the body, which is how a smaller judoka throws a much larger one. One clean throw ends the match outright, ippon. The jacket is part of the mechanism rather than a costume; it gives both fighters the handles the whole system is built on.

Jigoro Kano founded it in 1882 with twelve mats at the Eisho-ji temple in Tokyo, building it out of several jujutsu lines by removing the striking and the weapons and putting free sparring, randori, at the centre. Its reputation was won in the 1880s against rival jujutsu schools in police tournaments, and it entered the Olympics in 1964. Its exports outgrew it. Mitsuyo Maeda was teaching in Brazil by around 1914, which is where Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu comes from, and Vasili Oshchepkov took a Kodokan black belt home to Russia and folded judo into what became Sambo.

records.name: Karate (Goju-ryu)
records.tagline: Hard and soft — Naha-te breathing made into a school.
records.history:
Goju-ryu means hard-soft, and both halves are literal. The hard is straight closed-fist striking, and the soft is circular open-hand work that takes an incoming arm off its line instead of stopping it. It is fought close, inside the other person's reach, where the circles are small and there is nowhere to retreat to, so the answer to pressure is to redirect it rather than back away. All of it is organized around Sanchin, a short kata performed slowly under muscular tension with audible controlled breathing, which is the style's conditioning method and its signature at once.

Chōjun Miyagi built it out of Naha-te, which he began learning at fourteen under Kanryō Higaonna, and he made his own training trips to Fujian in 1915 and 1917. The name arrived almost by accident. In 1929 his student Jin'an Shinzato was asked at a demonstration what the art was called and had no answer, because Naha-te had never been a school name, so Miyagi took Goju from a line in the Bubishi about inhaling and exhaling. Mas Oyama trained under his senior student So Nei Chu before founding Kyokushin.

records.name: Karate (Kyokushin)
records.tagline: Full contact, no apology. Knockdown karate.
records.history:
Kyokushin fights bare-knuckle and trains the same way. No gloves, no shin pads, no headgear, so the hands and shins have to be conditioned into the weapons the rules already assume they are. Matches are full contact with kicks and knees allowed to the head and full power to the body and legs, but no punches to the face at all, because bare fists on an unprotected head would end bouts in seconds. That single exclusion shapes everything else. With no hand threat to the head, fighters stand close and trade, nobody has much reason to move backwards, and a bout is decided by body shots and low kicks landing until somebody's legs stop working, which is why the format is called knockdown karate.

Masutatsu Oyama was born Choi Yeong-eui in occupied Korea in 1923, studied Shotokan under Gichin Funakoshi, then spent several years with So Nei Chu, a senior Goju-ryu student of Chōjun Miyagi's. Shotokan's straight lines plus Goju-ryu's close-range power is roughly what he began teaching in 1953, founding the organization in April 1964. The format fed Seidokaikan, K-1 in 1993, and Kudo, and Kyokushin karateka like ONE FC's Yuki Yoza and Hiroki Akimoto are still among the most dangerous kickboxers competing.

records.name: Karate (Shito-ryu)
records.tagline: Shuri speed and Naha power, kept in one syllabus.
records.history:
Shito-ryu is the karate style that refused to choose. Shuri-te is direct and driving, worked at arm's length, while Naha-te is tighter, more circular, and fought close, with breathing and tension work Shuri-te has no use for. Most Okinawan karateka of that generation picked one and stayed inside it. Kenwa Mabuni kept both, which is why a Shito-ryu student learns long-range lines and short-range circles side by side, and why the style carries an unusually long kata list, somewhere between fifty and ninety depending on the branch.

Mabuni started under Ankō Itosu in Shuri at about thirteen, and his friend Chōjun Miyagi later introduced him to Kanryō Higaonna, so he took up Naha-te seriously as well. He moved to Osaka in 1929 to teach on the mainland and first called his approach Hanko-ryu, half-hard style, before settling on Shitō-ryū around 1931, assembled from the readings of the first characters in his two teachers' names: Shi from Itosu, Tō from Higaonna. It is one of the four styles recognized by the World Karate Federation.

records.name: Karate (Shotokan)
records.tagline: Long stances, straight lines — karate’s most-taught form.
records.history:
Shotokan is the long-range end of karate. The stances are deep and the techniques are big, which parks a fighter further out than most styles are comfortable with and then crosses that gap in one committed movement. Nothing about it is subtle, and that is deliberate; the deep stances are a training load before they are a fighting position, building the legs at a cost in mobility the style accepts on purpose. It is also the version most beginners meet, because large techniques performed in unison are the easiest thing in karate to teach to a full room.

Gichin Funakoshi trained in Shuri under Ankō Itosu, and in 1922 the Ministry of Education invited him to Tokyo to demonstrate at Japan's first national athletic exhibition. It went well enough that Jigoro Kano asked for a second performance at the Kodokan, after which Funakoshi simply stayed. The style owes as much to his son Yoshitaka, who pushed the kata toward those long, low stances. Students built him a dojo in Mejiro in 1936 and hung a sign reading Shoto-kan, his pen name joined to hall, a name he did not choose himself.

records.name: Karate (Wado-ryu)
records.tagline: Karate softened by jujutsu evasion — the way of harmony.
records.history:
Wado-ryu does not meet force with force. Where most karate stops an incoming strike with a hard block, Wado-ryu moves the whole body off the line the strike is travelling on, a shift called tai sabaki that evades and loads the counter in the same motion. That idea belongs to jujutsu rather than Okinawa, and it brings the rest of jujutsu with it; joint locks and throws sit in the syllabus beside the striking, and a practitioner is expected to end up behind an attacker rather than in front of one. The name translates to the way of harmony, which for once is a description.

Hironori Otsuka came to karate already a master of something else. He started Shindo Yoshin-ryu jujutsu at thirteen and by June 1921 held menkyo kaiden, full mastery and a licence to teach. He did not meet Gichin Funakoshi until the following year, and was among the first students Funakoshi promoted to black belt in 1924, though he also trained with Kenwa Mabuni and Choki Motobu, who had things to say about free sparring that a kata-centred syllabus did not cover. His own school opened in 1934.

records.name: Karate
records.founded: early 20th century (Okinawan roots trace to 15th century)
records.tagline: Empty hand — Okinawa’s answer, half native te, half Chinese fist.
records.history:
Karate is built around a single decisive strike, which is what separates it from the volume striking of boxing or Muay Thai. Power comes from the hips and the floor rather than the arm, travels in a straight line, and is pulled back as fast as it was sent, so the same limb is a threat again immediately. Even the blocks are strikes, aimed at the attacking arm rather than at absorbing the blow. Most of the material lives in kata, solo sequences run against imagined opponents, which is how an art with almost nothing written down survived several centuries intact.

It grew on Okinawa, then the independent Ryukyu Kingdom, out of a native practice called te crossed with Chinese methods carried back from Fujian, taking different shapes in Shuri, Naha, and Tomari. Anko Itosu put it into Shuri's school PE classes in 1901, and his student Gichin Funakoshi carried it to mainland Japan in the 1920s, borrowing judo's uniform and coloured belts along the way. In 1933 the character for kara was swapped from the one meaning China to a homophone meaning empty. Every major style below descends from it, and so do both branches of Taekwondo and Japanese kickboxing.

records.name: Kickboxing (Japan)
records.tagline: Karate that stopped pulling its punches, cut with Muay Thai.
records.history:
Kickboxing has two distinct lineages, albeit both being similar in style.

In Japan, the term "kickboxing" was first coined by Japanese boxing promoter Osamu Noguchi. The discipline itself, however, originated from Karate master Tatsuo Yamada. Inspired by the growth of Muay Thai and its similarities to Karate, Yamada looked to challenge his karateka students with Thailand's best fighters, thus prompting Noguchi to organize their first cross-discipline, full-contact sparring tournament between Japanese and Thai fighters in 1963. As the sport grew, Japanese fighters began trading techniques with the Thais and vice-versa. The rules began to mold as well, removing the Thai clinch from competition to favor a more forward-marching and faster paced fight than traditional Muay Thai's heavy footed competitions.

Today, kickboxing has grown into its own discipline, with schools opening up across the world teaching techniques derived from Muay Thai and Kickboxing, as well as borrowing from Taekwondo and Boxing. It is quite often you find fighters from different Karate disciplines, such as ONE FC's Yuki Yoza or Hiroki Akimoto (both trained in Kyokushin Karate) as well as Muay Thai fighters like Jonathan Haggerty and Tawanchai challenge themselves in kickboxing competitions.

records.name: Kickboxing (United States)
records.tagline: Point karate steps into a boxing ring, gloves on.
records.history:
Kickboxing has two distinct lineages, albeit both being similar in style.

The origin of American Kickboxing is far different from Japanese Kickboxing. Born in the 1970s, point-karate fighters grew tired of stopping the fight after every scored point. They felt that the essence of a true fight was beyond point-based rules and wanted to challenge themselves as they were inspired by the rise of boxing. The Professional Karate Association (PKA) instituted strict "above-the-waist" striking rules and banned low kicks (a technique commonly seen in Asian kickboxing). This, however, led to a high-volume, dynamic kicking spectacle. The bladed Karate stance combined with the coaching from American boxers led to historical striking matches that many modern day fighters study today.

records.name: Kudo
records.tagline: Karate, judo and the clinch in one full-contact art.
records.history:
Kudo solved karate's face-punch problem with equipment. Fighters wear a clear moulded helmet, and behind it the rules open all the way up: full-contact strikes standing, judo throws, and ground work with a short clock before the referee stands everyone back up. It also does something almost no other combat sport does about size. Competitors are matched on an index that adds height in centimetres to weight in kilograms, so a tall light fighter and a short heavy one land in the same bracket, and reach is treated as an advantage worth counting rather than an accident of the weigh-in.

Takashi Azuma came up through judo, joined Mas Oyama's Kyokushin organization in 1971, and won the All Japan in 1977, where other fighters called him the human locomotive for his low kicks. He retired in 1979 with a complaint: facing larger opponents abroad had convinced him that Kyokushin's rules, no face punches and no throws, left a smaller man no way to close the gap. On 17 February 1981 he founded Daido Juku in Sendai, striking from Kyokushin and grappling from judo, and renamed the system Kudo in 2001.

records.name: Muay Thai
records.founded: 18th century (documented); disputed roots to 13th century; codified as ring sport 1920s to 1930s
records.tagline: The art of eight limbs — fists, elbows, knees, shins.
records.history:
Growing in popularity due to the recent rise of the promotion of ONE FC, Muay Thai is considered by many to be the absolute peak of striking martial arts. Unlike traditional western boxing which is restricted by two points of contact, or Muay Thai's sister system kickboxing with its four points of contact, the "art of eight limbs" utilizes one's hands, legs, knees, and elbows in competition. It is also unique in its devastating roundhouse kick that differs from the likes of Taekwondo or Karate, opting to strike with the shin bone rather than the foot.

Originating in Thailand, Muay Thai is deeply rooted in tradition and ritual with fighters performing the Wai Kru (a ritual dance) to pay respect to their teachers and ancestors; a ritual still performed today. Historians note that the system derived from the training of unarmed combat used by soldiers in the 13th-18th century. Today, many MMA fighters choose to study Muay Thai as their base of striking due to its effectiveness when on the feet.

records.name: Sambo
records.tagline: The Red Army’s grappling, drilled from judo and folk wrestling.
records.history:
Sambo is jacket wrestling with the leg locks left in. The kurtka gives grips much like a judo jacket, but the shorts and wrestling boots underneath say where the rest of it came from. Heel hooks, kneebars, and ankle locks were legal from the start, at a point when judo had already ruled most of them out, and sport sambo bans chokes outright, which pushes a match further toward the legs than any comparable art. Combat sambo puts the strikes back in and is a different animal entirely.

Unlike most martial arts, it was commissioned. The Red Army wanted better hand-to-hand training in the early 1920s, and Vasili Oshchepkov, who had studied judo in Japan under Jigoro Kano, spent the decade blending judo with Soviet folk wrestling while Viktor Spiridonov worked on a softer system at Dynamo in Moscow. Oshchepkov did not live to see it recognized, arrested in the Great Purge in 1937 on a fabricated spying charge and dead in custody, and the credit in 1938 went largely to his student Anatoly Kharlampiev. The name abbreviates samozashchita bez oruzhiya, self-defence without weapons.

records.name: Silat
records.founded: unknown (Minangkabau tradition traces origins to the 6th century)
records.tagline: Low stances, sudden angles, hidden blades — origins disputed with Malaysia.
records.history:
Silat is a family of arts rather than a single one, spread across Indonesia and Malaysia in versions that share a logic without sharing a confirmed lineage — this entry follows the Indonesian branch, though credible tradition also places roots on the Malay side. Pencak silat, is a blade art that trains empty-handed. The kris, the golok, and the hooked karambit sit behind the syllabus even when there is nothing in the hand, which is why so much of it goes after limbs and joints rather than the head, and why the footwork drops so low. The langkah step patterns move along triangles and squares marked on the floor, cutting angles to get outside an attack rather than retreating from it.

There is no founder and no founding date, and the early history moved by mouth across Sumatra and Java. Tradition places the beginning among the Minangkabau of West Sumatra, whose hulubalang bodyguards were said to be training in structured fighting by the 6th century. What is documented is the variety: Cimande, a close-quarters West Java system, was taught publicly by around 1760, and Merpati Putih came out of 17th-century royal courts and is now the armed forces' standard unarmed system. IPSI, founded in 1948, is the oldest national silat body in the world.

records.name: Taekwondo (ITF)
records.tagline: The way of the fist and the foot — Korea’s high kick.
records.history:
ITF Taekwondo is the older and more traditional of the sport's two branches, organized around its patterns. There are twenty-four of them, tul, one for each hour of the day, and they hold the syllabus the way kata hold karate's. The technical argument that separates this branch from the Olympic one is a motion called sine wave, where the body rises and then drops through each technique, on the theory that dropping one's own mass into a strike generates power differently from the hip snap Seoul teaches. Sparring is light-contact and fought at long range with the hands kept low, because at that distance the legs get there first.

Taekwondo got its name in 1955, when the leaders of Korea's postwar kwans agreed to unify, and General Choi Hong Hi pushed hardest for it. The Korea Taekwondo Association formalized the merger in 1959, and Choi walked out in 1966 to found the International Taekwon-Do Federation, adding sine wave around 1980. The politics never left the art. After Seoul blocked him from teaching in North Korea he moved his headquarters to Toronto in 1972 and Vienna in 1985, and he died in Pyongyang in 2002.

records.name: Taekwondo (WT/Kukkiwon)
records.tagline: Olympic taekwondo — sport kicking, refined at the Kukkiwon.
records.history:
WT Taekwondo and Taekwondo itself in the martial arts world is considered to contain the peak of kicking techniques, displaying levels of flexibility and expanded kicking potential beyond the likes of Muay Thai or Karate. Its spinning kicks, heavy axe kicks, and hook kicks make a Taekwondo fighter extremely difficult to fight from long-range.

Formerly branded "World Taekwondo Federation" or WTF Taekwondo, WT Taekwondo formed after the Japanese occupation of Korea ended in 1945. Korean martial arts masters merged the techniques of kick-heavy traditional Taekkyeon with the foundations of Shotokan Karate, unifying the arts under "kwans" or martial arts schools. General Choi Hong Hi formed the International Taekwondo Federation as one governed style, though the political rift between the north and south led to the WTF and both schools drifting stylistically.

The sport's introduction to the Olympics, combined with the migration from human judging to electronic sensors for scoring, is what many believe to be a sort of "degradation" of the sport. With electronic sensors requiring only an exact impact threshold to register points, the physical "meta" of sparring competition turned from its traditional raw power and heavy kicking fights (resulting often in knockouts to end competition), to lighter "fencing" like matches with fighters simply tapping their foot to make contact and score a point. Its Poomsae, the competition of choreographed routines, are still an amazing spectacle to see regardless of cultist opinions on the art itself, featuring wild acts of board breaking and displays of strength and creativity beyond its sparring potential.

records.name: Wing Chun
records.tagline: Close-range southern kung fu built on centerline control.
records.history:
Wing Chun fights in a corridor. Everything is arranged around the centreline, an imaginary vertical line down the middle of the body, and the rule is to take it and keep it, striking straight down the middle on the shortest path available so the attacking arm is already sitting where a block would go. It works close, near enough that hands are felt rather than seen. Chi sao, sticking hands, drills exactly that, with two people joined at the forearms reading pressure and following it.

Who built it is unknown, and at least eight lineages tell the story differently. The version told most often has a Shaolin nun, Ng Mui, teaching a young woman named Yim Wing-chun, though she is treated as a mythical originator rather than a person with a record. The first well-documented practitioner is Leung Jan, a Foshan herbalist who began teaching privately around 1870; his student Chan Wah-shun later trained a boy named Ip Man, who moved to Hong Kong around 1949 and opened the art to the public there. Bruce Lee was one of Ip Man's Hong Kong students, and he eventually judged the art too rigid, building Jeet Kune Do out of that criticism. You might've seen Wing Chun's growth through the "Ip Man" films, Donnie Yen's biopic series starting in 2008 that turned Ip Man himself into the art's global face.

records.name: Wrestling
records.founded: prehistoric, no single origin (earliest depictions c. 15,000-17,000 BCE)
records.tagline: No founder, no homeland — humanity’s oldest contest.
records.history:
Wrestling is the art of controlling a person without hurting them, and it is the most borrowed system in all of combat sport. No strikes, no chokes, no joint locks; the entire contest is position. Take the opponent down, turn them, and in freestyle and folkstyle end it by pinning both shoulders to the mat. Grips are taken on the body rather than on clothing, so nothing slows an exchange down. Every system that ends up on the ground has to answer the question of who gets to be on top, and wrestling is the answer all of them use.

It has no founder and no homeland, appearing in cave art in France fifteen thousand years ago and in the ancient Olympics by 708 BCE. Since no country can claim it, this entry follows documented dominance instead. Georgia's chidaoba carries roughly 200 named holds and is still its most successful Olympic event, and the Soviet system took 116 Olympic medals, a legacy sharpest in Dagestan, a republic of about 3.1 million people with more than twenty Olympic golds since 1992, which is why the marker sits on Makhachkala.
